title: Letters to a friend
hook: late in life, Seneca writes 124 letters to Lucilius, a friend in Sicily, about living well

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Discourses close, and your line was thank you, teacher. Did you write Epictetus his line? Day four hundred thirty-one. A new part of the porch begins.

Somewhere in a drawer, or a shoebox, or an old email account, you may have a letter someone wrote only to you. Not a group message. Not a post. A letter, with your name at the top, written by someone who was thinking about you while they wrote it. Those are the ones people keep. Almost two thousand years ago, an old and powerful Roman stepped back from public life and started writing letters like that to one friend. People are still reading them. Today: letters to a friend.
screen: `A LETTER WITH YOUR NAME ON IT.` → `THE ONES PEOPLE KEEP.` → `LETTERS TO A FRIEND.`

segments.voice: First, the writer. Lucius Annaeus Seneca was born in Corduba, in Spain, around the time of Jesus' birth. He became a famous writer in Rome, was exiled, was called back, and became tutor and then advisor to the young emperor Nero. He grew very rich. He lived, in other words, right in the middle of everything the Stoics warned about, and he knew it. Around the year sixty-two he asked to withdraw from Nero's court. Second, the friend. Lucilius was a younger man serving as a Roman official in Sicily, a writer himself, interested in philosophy. Seneca writes to him as an equal who is a few steps behind on the same path. Every letter opens the same way, in Latin: Seneca to his Lucilius, greetings. Third, the letters. A hundred twenty-four survive, gathered in twenty books, written in the last few years of Seneca's life. They're short. Each one usually takes something ordinary, a trip, a cold bath, a noisy apartment, a visit to an old house, and turns it into a lesson about how to live. Scholars still argue whether Lucilius really received them all or whether Seneca wrote them to be published. Either way, they're written to one person. Fourth, the ending. In the year sixty-five Nero accused Seneca of joining a plot against him and ordered him to die. The letters were written with that shadow already falling. That's why they're urgent and tender at once. For the next stretch of the path, we'll read them in order, a letter at a time, as if they were addressed to us.
screen: `SENECA: RICH, POWERFUL, UNEASY.` · `LUCILIUS, A FRIEND IN SICILY.` · `124 SHORT LETTERS ABOUT LIVING.` · `WRITTEN IN THE LAST YEARS.` · then, large: `DEAR FRIEND.`

segments.voice: Think of one friend you haven't really written to in a while. Not a quick text. Picture them at their kitchen table, opening something from you. Now, in your head or on paper, begin: dear, and their name. Write two or three sentences. Something you noticed this week. Something you've been thinking about. Something you hope for them. You don't have to send it yet. Just let yourself write to one person, the way Seneca did. The bell holds the time.
Letters to a friend. Seneca's hundred twenty-four letters to Lucilius, written in his last years, each one turning an ordinary day into a lesson about living well. Today's word.
Your line: dear friend. Finish your short letter today, a few honest lines to one person, and send it. Day four hundred thirty-one.

howItsDone: Many readers work through Seneca's letters one at a time, often a letter a day, and some keep up the habit of writing reflective letters to a friend.

trapdoor: what you thought: old letters are just history.
what it means: Seneca's letters to Lucilius are short lessons in living, written to one friend in the last years of his life.
what a scholar hears: 124 letters survive in twenty books; Aulus Gellius quotes a 'book twenty-two', so some of the collection is lost.

notes: Seneca's birth in Corduba c. 4 BCE–1 CE ('around the time of Jesus' birth'); exile to Corsica under Claudius (41), recall (49), tutor and advisor to Nero; request to withdraw in 62 (Tacitus, Annals 14.52–56); death in 65 after the Pisonian conspiracy (Annals 15.60–64). Confirm.
Lucilius as procurator in Sicily: from the letters themselves (e.g. Letter 79); confirm.
124 letters in 20 books; Aulus Gellius (Attic Nights 12.2) cites a 22nd book. Confirm.
